title: Leadership Styles and Influence
keyIdea: There is more than one way to lead. A directive leader gives clear orders. A democratic leader lets the group decide. A servant leader asks what people need and helps. A transformational leader shares a goal that inspires. No style is always best: pick the one that fits the moment. Good leaders also make room for quiet voices, and they influence people with reasons, never with threats, tricks or pressure. A yes given out of fear is not a free choice.
familyTip: Talk about a team, club or group you have both been in. Who led it, and how? When did that style work, and when did it not? Then ask: what is the difference between persuading someone and pressuring them?

visual.caption: Which leadership style is each leader using? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: “Hands up for the film you want.”
“How can I make your job easier?”
“Let’s be the first class to win the green flag.”

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name four styles, match them to situations, get quiet voices heard, sort persuasion from pressure and lead a team with trust and effort meters.

kid: Leading is not just being the boss. There are different styles. A directive leader gives clear orders. A democratic leader lets the group decide, often by a vote. A servant leader asks what others need, then helps them. A transformational leader shares a big goal that makes people want to grow.

No style is best all the time. In a fire drill you need fast orders, not a vote. When the class picks a trip, everyone should get a say. When a friend is stuck, they need help, not a speech. Good leaders switch style to fit the moment.
In most groups a few people do most of the talking. That does not mean they have the best ideas. A good leader asks quiet people by name, or goes round the circle so everyone gets a turn.

Leaders have influence, and that comes with a duty. Fair influence gives reasons and leaves people free to say no. Threats, shaming, fake crowds and secrets are pressure. They may work for a moment, but trust falls. If someone says yes only because they are scared, that is not real consent.
adult: This fits the PSHE Association plan for Key Stage 3: healthy relationships, speaking up for yourself, peer influence and spotting coercion. It also fits the DfE guidance on respectful relationships and consent. The four styles are the usual school model. Directive and democratic come from studies of boys' clubs by Lewin and his team in 1939. Servant leadership is from Greenleaf (1970). Transformational leadership is from Burns (1978) and Bass (1985). The idea that the best style depends on the task comes from Hersey and Blanchard.

The lab treats including quiet people as a skill to practise. In most group talks a few people take most of the time. A question thrown to the whole room is mostly answered by the most confident. Asking by name, going round the circle, or writing ideas down first gives everyone a turn, and it brings out ideas that were there all along.

Common mistakes: thinking one style is always right; thinking a leader must be loud or bossy; calling threats or public shaming 'being firm'; missing fake crowd pressure or a request for secrecy as tricks; and thinking a yes counts as consent even when it came from fear. Say clearly that pressure from a friend or partner is never their fault, and that they can always talk to a trusted adult.

practice.prompt: “Fire alarm. Everyone out the side door, now.” Which style is this?
practice.hint: Who decides here, and is there time to talk?
practice.explain: The leader gives clear, fast orders. That is directive, and it is right in an emergency.

practice.prompt: A teammate is stuck and stressed the night before a deadline. Which style fits best?
choices: Servant: ask what they need and help
Democratic: let the group vote on it
practice.hint: What does a stuck, stressed person need most?
practice.explain: A servant leader removes what is blocking someone. Orders or a vote do not unstick them.

practice.prompt: A group of {n} people meets. Only 2 of them have spoken. How many people have not been heard yet?
practice.hint: Take the people who have spoken from the whole group.
practice.explain: {n} − 2 = {=n-2} people have not spoken. A good leader asks them by name or goes round the circle.

practice.prompt: In a go-round, each of {n} people gets {t} minutes to share an idea. How many minutes does the go-round take?
practice.hint: Everyone gets the same time. Multiply.
practice.explain: {n} × {t} = {=n*t} minutes. Fair shares of time stop two voices taking over.

practice.prompt: “Do it or you are out of the group chat.” What is this?
practice.hint: Does it give a reason, or threaten a loss?
practice.explain: It threatens to exclude someone if they refuse. That is coercion. A yes given to avoid it is not a free choice.

pool.prompt: Which leadership style is the best one?
pool.hint: Think of a fire drill, then of choosing a class trip.
pool.explain: Each style fits some moments. Good leaders switch: orders in danger, a vote for shared choices, help for someone stuck.

pool.prompt: Two people do all the talking in a meeting. What should the leader do?
pool.hint: Who answers an open question to the whole room?
pool.explain: Open questions are usually answered by the same confident people. Asking by name, or a go-round, brings in new ideas.

choices: “Here is why it matters. You can still say no.”
pool.hint: Fair influence gives reasons and leaves the choice free.
pool.explain: Reasons plus a free choice is persuasion. A fake crowd is pressure, and secrecy from trusted adults is a warning sign.

pool.prompt: A friend says yes only because they are scared to say no. Is that real consent?
choices: No: consent has to be freely given
Yes, if it is a small thing
pool.hint: Could they have said no with nothing bad happening?
pool.explain: Consent means a free choice. A yes given out of fear or pressure is not consent, whatever the size of the thing.

choices: They share a goal that inspires people to grow
They let everyone do what they like
pool.hint: Transform means change. What do they change in their team?
pool.explain: A transformational leader paints a shared goal that makes people want to do more and get better.

pool.prompt: A team leader threatens to tell the teacher who is lazy. Effort goes up. What usually happens next?
choices: Trust falls, and people stop helping when not watched
pool.hint: Do people trust someone who threatens them?
pool.explain: Threats can buy effort for a moment, but trust drops. People do the minimum and drift away.

pool.prompt: In a vote, {y} people pick the beach and {p} pick the park. How many more people chose the beach?
pool.hint: Find the difference between the two numbers.
pool.explain: {y} − {p} = {=y-p}. A democratic leader goes with the vote, and makes sure the others felt heard.

pool.prompt: A leader agrees with Ben in front of him, then changes the plan back in secret. What is this?
pool.hint: Is it honest? Does Ben really get a say?
pool.explain: Pretending to agree and then going behind his back is manipulation. When Ben finds out, trust collapses.

pool.prompt: A club of {n} people does a go-round. Before it, {q} people had not spoken. How many people had spoken before the go-round?
pool.hint: Take the quiet people away from the whole club.
pool.explain: {n} − {q} = {=n-q} had spoken. The go-round gave the other {q} a turn too.
